In [[complex analysis]], a branch of mathematics, the '''residue at infinity''' is a [[Residue (complex analysis)|residue]] of a [[holomorphic function]] on an [[Annulus (mathematics)|annulus]] having an infinite external radius.  The ''infinity'' <math>\infty</math> is a point added to the local space <math>\mathbb C </math> in order to render it [[compact space|compact]] (in this case it is a [[Alexandroff extension|one-point compactification]]). This space denoted <math> \hat{\mathbb C} </math> is [[isomorphism|isomorphic]] to the [[Riemann sphere]].<ref>Michèle Audin, ''Analyse Complexe'', lecture notes of the University of Strasbourg [http://www-irma.u-strasbg.fr/~maudin/analysecomp.pdf available on the web] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120125164622/http://www-irma.u-strasbg.fr/%7Emaudin/analysecomp.pdf |date=2012-01-25 }}, pp. 70–72</ref> One can use the residue at infinity to calculate some [[integral]]s.

==Definition==
Given a holomorphic function ''f'' on an [[Annulus (mathematics)|annulus]] <math> A(0, R, \infty) </math> (centered at 0, with inner radius <math>R</math> and infinite outer radius), the '''residue at infinity''' of the function ''f'' can be defined in terms of the usual [[residue (mathematics)|residue]] as follows:

:<math> \operatorname{Res}(f,\infty) = -\operatorname{Res}\left( {1\over z^2}f\left({1\over z}\right), 0  \right).</math>

Thus, one can transfer the study of <math> f(z) </math> at infinity to the study of <math> f(1/z) </math> at the origin.

Note that <math>\forall r > R</math>, we have

:<math> \operatorname{Res}(f, \infty) = {-1\over 2\pi i}\int_{C(0, r)} f(z) \, dz.</math>
Since, for holomorphic functions the sum of the residues at the isolated singularities plus the residue at infinity is zero, it can be expressed as:

<math> \operatorname{Res}(f(z), \infty) = -\sum_k \operatorname{Res}\left(f\left(z\right), a_k\right).</math>

==Motivation==

One might first guess that the definition of the residue of <math>f(z)</math> at infinity should just be the residue of <math>f(1/z)</math> at <math>z=0</math>. However, the reason that we consider instead <math>-\frac{1}{z^2}f\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)</math> is that one does not take residues of ''functions'', but of ''[[Differential form|differential forms]]'', i.e. the residue of <math>f(z)dz</math> at infinity is the residue of <math>f\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)d\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)=-\frac{1}{z^2}f\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)dz</math> at <math>z=0</math>.
